title: Seven days of silence
hook: his friends sit silent with him seven days, their finest hour (Job 2:13)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Job: a blameless man who loses everything, and the reader is told first it isn't punishment. Your line was it wasn't deserved. Today, his friends arrive.

At a wake, a slow line of people moves past the family. Each one leans in and says something. I'm so sorry. She was a lovely woman. Call me if you need anything. Then somebody reaches the front, takes a hand in both of theirs, and says nothing at all. Just holds on, stays a moment, and moves along. Saying nothing can be the hardest thing in that line to do. In the book of Job, three friends do exactly that, and for a long time.
screen: `A SLOW LINE AT A WAKE.` → `SOMEONE SAYS NOTHING AT ALL.` → `THREE FRIENDS DO EXACTLY THAT.`

segments.voice: First, they come. Three of Job's friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, hear of everything that has fallen on him. Each sets out from his own place; they had made an appointment together "to come to mourn with him and to comfort him." Before a word is said, they make a plan, and they travel. Second, they don't know him. From far off they look up and can't recognize their friend. So they raise their voices and weep. Each tears his robe. They throw dust into the air, over their heads, toward heaven. Their mourning is loud and physical before it's anything else. Third, they sit down. "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." Upon the ground, with him, at his level, not standing over him. Day and night, and nobody fills the air. Fourth, silence that comes from seeing. The verse gives one reason for the quiet: they saw how great the grief was. Some readers take it that words would have been too small for it. Some call this the friends' finest hour, partly because of what happens when they finally open their mouths. But that's tomorrow. For now: they came, they wept, they sat on the ground where he was, and they kept quiet because they could see.
screen: `THEY COME, BY APPOINTMENT.` · `THEY CAN'T RECOGNIZE HIM.` · `THEY SIT ON THE GROUND WITH HIM.` · `SILENCE THAT COMES FROM SEEING.` · then, large: `SIT WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: Settle down low if you can, feet flat or even on the floor, and bring to mind someone who is hurting right now. In your mind, go and sit next to them on the ground, at their level, and say nothing: no advice, no reasons, no it'll be okay. If words come up, let them pass like a car outside, and keep seeing them.
Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends who sat with him on the ground seven days and nights without a word, because they saw his grief. Today's word.
Your line: sit with them. Sometimes the quiet, kept close, is the comfort. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Jewish and Christian readers take Job 2:11–13 as a picture of comforting mourners; in Jewish mourning custom, visitors come to sit with the bereaved, and tradition has visitors wait for the mourner to speak first.

notes: Editor: 'understood that words would be too small' (beyond the text's 'for they saw') now attributed to some readers; practice dropped 'see their face', which repeated day 705's practice.
Job 2:12 paraphrased: they lifted up their eyes afar off, knew him not, lifted up their voice and wept, rent their mantles, sprinkled dust upon their heads toward heaven.
'Their finest hour' (from the outline) is attributed to 'some readers'.

howItsDone mentions Jewish mourning custom (visitors sit with the bereaved and wait for the mourner to speak first) without naming shiva or its length; a Judaism Keeper should confirm the wording or cut it.
